entries.title: Barranco León and Fuente Nueva-3 establish 1.4 Ma hominin presence in southeastern Spain
entries.dateMeaning: Combined paleomagnetic, ESR, and biochronological envelope in the Guadix-Baza Basin
entries.summary: Mode 1 limestone-flint choppers, cut-marked hippopotamus and mammoth bones, and the BL02-J54-100 deciduous molar mark Europe's oldest Iberian hominin site.
entries.detail: Toro-Moyano et al. (2013), Yravedra et al. (2022), and Gibert et al. (2024) substantiate early Oldowan hominin foraging around Orce's mineral-rich Pleistocene lakeshores.
entries.uncertainty: Dating within reverse Matuyama polarity intervals retains a ±100-kyr geochronological bracket.

entries.title: Atapuerca's Sima del Elefante TE7–TE9 yields Western Europe's oldest human face
entries.dateMeaning: Cosmogenic nuclide burial, ESR, and magnetostratigraphic age envelope in Trinchera del Elefante
entries.place: Sierra de Atapuerca, Burgos, Castile and León
entries.summary: Alongside flake tools and cut-marked fauna in TE9 (~1.2 Ma), lower level TE7 preserved the ATE7-1 mid-face maxilla between 1.4 and 1.1 Ma.
entries.detail: Carbonell et al. (2008) and Huguet et al. (2025) demonstrate archaic *Homo* morphology predating *Homo antecessor* along the upper Duero–Ebro watershed.
entries.uncertainty: Fragmentary facial anatomy in ATE7-1 leaves exact species attribution between early Eurasian *Homo* lineages open.

entries.title: Barranc de la Boella documents ~1 Ma Acheulean large cutting tools in Catalonia
entries.dateMeaning: Cosmogenic 26Al/10Be and paleomagnetic Jaramillo–Matuyama bracket in Unit II
entries.summary: Fluvial-deltaic beds at Barranc de la Boella preserve an early Acheulean pick and cleaver workshop alongside butchered mammoth carcasses.
entries.detail: Vallverdú et al. (2014) dated Early Pleistocene large cutting tools near Tarragona, pushing western European Acheulean handaxe arrival near one million years ago.
entries.uncertainty: Scatter in cosmogenic burial pairs retains a ~200-kyr statistical error envelope.

entries.title: Gran Dolina preserves ~850 ka Homo antecessor remains and later Acheulean hunting layers
entries.dateMeaning: Age span bridging TD6 (~850–770 ka H. antecessor) through TD10 (~450–300 ka bison camps)
entries.summary: Aurora Stratum TD6 held defleshed *Homo antecessor* fossils below later TD10 communal bison-hunting and early Levallois pavements.
entries.detail: Welker et al. (2020) extracted dental enamel proteins positioning *H. antecessor* near the last common ancestor of modern humans, Neanderthals, and Denisovans.
entries.uncertainty: Discontinuous cave sedimentation creates multi-millennia hiatuses between TD6 and TD10 horizons.

entries.title: Sima de los Huesos yields ~430 ka nuclear DNA from early Neanderthal-lineage kin
entries.dateMeaning: Combined luminescence, U-series, and paleomagnetic bracket for over 28 accumulated individuals
entries.place: Cueva Mayor, Sierra de Atapuerca, Burgos
entries.summary: Stacked at the bottom of a 13-meter vertical shaft with a finely flaked red quartzite biface ("Excalibur"), ~29 individuals preserve early Neanderthal traits.
entries.detail: Meyer et al. (2016) recovered partial nuclear DNA showing these Middle Pleistocene hominins had already diverged along the Neanderthal sister branch away from Denisovans.
entries.uncertainty: Whether deposition reflects deliberate funerary tossing or catastrophic mass mortality remains debated.

entries.title: Cova Negra preserves Middle Pleistocene Neanderthal child survival in Valencia
entries.dateMeaning: Chronostratigraphic bracket for Levantine Mousterian karst levels
entries.summary: Deep Mousterian levels at Cova Negra yielded cranial fragments showing congenital inner-ear pathology in a Neanderthal child cared for past infancy.
entries.detail: Middle Pleistocene paleoanthropological syntheses (Harvati & Reyes-Centeno 2022) group Cova Negra with early Mediterranean Neanderthal populations.
entries.uncertainty: Historic trench excavations create wide radiometric brackets around individual juvenile specimens.

entries.title: Travertine ledges at Abric Romaní cast ~70–40 ka Neanderthal wooden tools
entries.dateMeaning: U-series travertine sheet dates interleaving hearth-centered Neanderthal camps
entries.summary: Calcium-carbonate springs rapidly sealed hearths and negative pseudomorph molds of sculpted pine spears, dishes, and digging sticks.
entries.detail: Mateo-Lomba et al. (2024) and Saladié et al. (2026) document specialized Neanderthal carpentry, bone projectile tips, and organized camp zoning.
entries.uncertainty: Upper levels approach radiocarbon saturation limits near 40 ka.

entries.title: El Sidrón and Prado Vargas preserve Neanderthal kinship genetics and curation behavior
entries.dateMeaning: AMS radiocarbon and luminescence ages across northern Iberian Mousterian karst caves
entries.summary: Dental calculus, patrilocal kinship genetics from twelve individuals at El Sidrón, and curated Cretaceous marine fossils at Prado Vargas widen Neanderthal behavioral records.
entries.detail: Vernot et al. (2021) recovered ancient nuclear DNA directly from cave sediments while Ruíz et al. (2024) documented non-utilitarian fossil collection.
entries.uncertainty: Secondary karst transport moved El Sidrón bones before final burial.

entries.title: Gorham's and Vanguard Caves chronicle coastal Mediterranean Neanderthal survival
entries.dateMeaning: Luminescence and radiocarbon bracket across sea-cave Mousterian hearths
entries.summary: Living beside exposed coastal plains, Iberian Neanderthals exploited shellfish, seabirds, and marine mammals while engraving cross-hatched bedrock marks.
entries.detail: Listed under WHC No. 1500 and framed by Villalba-Mouco et al. (2023), southern Iberia anchored Pleistocene continuity before LGM refugium turnover.
entries.uncertainty: Uppermost Mousterian hearth radiocarbon ages around 32–28 ka remain scrutinized for subtle young-carbon contamination.

entries.title: Cantabrian caves from El Castillo to Altamira span 39 ka disks to Magdalenian bison murals
entries.dateMeaning: U-series carbonate crusts overlying red disks at El Castillo (~40.8 ka cal) through LGM/Magdalenian polychromes
entries.place: Altamira, El Castillo & El Mirón, Cantabria
entries.summary: From Aurignacian–pre-Aurignacian red pigment disks to Altamira's polychrome bison ceiling and the El Mirón "Red Lady" burial, Cantabria records unbroken Paleolithic tradition.
entries.detail: Pike et al. (2012) dated minimum calcite crusts in eleven Spanish caves while Gelabert et al. (2025) tracked sedimentary ancient DNA through the Late Pleistocene at El Mirón.
entries.uncertainty: U-series calcite crusts supply minimum age ceilings rather than the day pigment touched bedrock.

entries.title: Cueva del Malalmuerzo anchors Iberia's Ice Age refugium genetic continuity
entries.dateMeaning: Direct radiocarbon and genome age on the Malalmuerzo Solutrean individual
entries.summary: A ~23,000-year-old human individual from Malalmuerzo links older western European Aurignacian-Gravettian lineages directly to post-LGM Magdalenian populations.
entries.detail: Villalba-Mouco et al. (2023) demonstrate that southern Iberia served as an unbroken genetic refugium when northern Europe emptied or experienced population replacement at peak cold.
entries.uncertainty: Single-site ancient genomes sample individual ancestry rather than regional census density.

entries.title: Cardial coastal settlers plant early Neolithic farming in eastern Iberia
entries.dateMeaning: Calibrated radiocarbon bracket across Catalan and Valencian Cardial cave/open settlements
entries.summary: Arriving swiftly by sea via the Gulf of Lion, Cardial farmers introduced naked wheat, barley, sheep, and shell-stamped vessels across Mediterranean valleys.
entries.detail: Hamon et al. (2021) trace parallel maritime colonization routes leapfrogging coastal lagoons between southeastern France, Valencia, and Andalusian capes.
entries.uncertainty: Marine reservoir effects on shell artifacts require terrestrial seed calibration where preserved.

entries.title: Bastioned walls and corbelled tholoi rise at Copper Age Los Millares
entries.dateMeaning: Radiocarbon sequence of concentric fortification lines, outer forts, and >80 tholos tombs
entries.place: Santa Fe de Mondújar, Almería, SE Spain
entries.summary: Controlling copper smelting and arid Andarax terraces, Los Millares erected three concentric limestone curtain walls, semi-circular bastions, and outlying watch-forts.
entries.detail: Barruezo-Vaquero et al. (2022) produced millimeter-resolution 3-D and GIS reconstructions of Los Millares's walled spur and necropolis.
entries.uncertainty: Internal village chronology across peripheral Hillforts 1–13 remains sampled selectively.

entries.title: El Argar hillforts forge Europe's earliest Bronze Age palace-like hierarchy
entries.dateMeaning: Bayesian radiocarbon range from La Bastida, La Almoloya, and El Argar acropoleis
entries.summary: Fortified hilltops and silver-diadem intramural jar burials reveal sharp social stratification, standardized halberds, and frontier exchange across southeastern Iberia.
entries.detail: Gil et al. (2025) map ceramic circulation and frontier economies separating Argaric polities from northern Bronze Age communities.
entries.uncertainty: Extent of centralized tribute versus confederated hilltop autonomy remains debated across western Murcia valleys.

entries.title: Gadir and Tartessos fuse Phoenician Atlantic voyaging with Iberian silver metallurgy
entries.dateMeaning: Ninth-century BCE Phoenician sanctuary horizons at Cádiz to Second Punic War Roman capture
entries.summary: Levantine Phoenician mariners raised temples to Melqart on Cádiz islands to refine Rio Tinto and Tartessian silver for Mediterranean–Atlantic shipping.
entries.detail: Castellano et al. (2018) and Villarías Robles et al. (2024) pair coastal geoarchaeology at Cádiz and the Guadalquivir paleogulf with classical *Ora Maritima* traditions.
entries.uncertainty: Deep Holocene estuarine silting buries portions of the early Guadalquivir Tartessian archipelago.

entries.title: Mazarrón and Bajo de la Campana wrecks preserve Phoenician tin, ivory, and sewn hulls
entries.dateMeaning: Seventh–sixth-century BCE Phoenician ceramic and cargo associations off Murcia
entries.place: Mazarrón & Bajo de la Campana reefs, Murcia coast
entries.summary: Remarkable seventh-century Phoenician wrecks preserve intact small boat joinery at Mazarrón and carved elephant tusks alongside tin ingots off Cartagena.
entries.detail: Pomey (2019) and Bachhuber (2019) synthesize Phoenician western silver-tin shipping networks captured on Spanish coastal reefs.
entries.uncertainty: Cargo origin stops reflect port-of-loading mixes spanning North Africa, central Mediterranean, and Iberian mines.

entries.title: Qart Hadasht fortification and the 219 BCE siege of Saguntum ignite the Second Punic War
entries.dateMeaning: Hasdrubal's founding of Qart Hadasht (Cartagena, 228) and Hannibal's Saguntum siege (219) to Scipio's 209 capture
entries.summary: Fortifying Cartagena's deep natural harbor to finance Iberian armies, the Barcids besieged Roman-allied Saguntum for eight months, triggering Hannibal's march on Italy.
entries.detail: Excavated Punic ashlar walls at Cartagena (Victoria et al. 2024) pair directly with Polybius Book III's account of Saguntum and Punic Iberia.
entries.uncertainty: Pre-Roman Ebro treaty boundaries remain interpreted through later Roman diplomatic polemics.

participants: Barcid Carthaginian forces under Hannibal Barca
Saguntine defenders; later Roman forces under Scipio Africanus
warfare.outcome: Capture of Saguntum sparked war with Rome before Scipio seized Qart Hadasht itself in 209 BCE.

entries.title: Via Augusta integrates Roman Tarraco, Córdoba, and Gades along a 1,500 km highway
entries.dateLabel: Augustan imperial milestone consolidation (c. 8 BCE–450 CE)
entries.dateMeaning: Imperial consolidation from Iberian coastal tracks to Cádiz recorded at Mengíbar Ianus Augustus and Itiner-e
entries.summary: Connecting Catalonia across Baetica to the Atlantic straits, the Via Augusta linked silver mines, river ports, and Roman veteran coloniae.
entries.detail: Gutiérrez Rodríguez et al. (2022), Castillo Pascual (2023), and de Soto et al. (2025) detail road stratigraphy and Baetis (Guadalquivir) river-road interchanges.
entries.uncertainty: Schematic highway connects provincial termini Tarraco and Gades across pre-existing Iberian Via Heraclea routes.

entries.title: Las Médulas hydraulic mines and Segovia's granite aqueduct transform Hispania
entries.dateMeaning: Flavian-Trajanic imperial gold mining peaks in León alongside Segovia aqueduct masonry
entries.summary: Roman engineers breached mountains with *ruina montium* pressurized water tanks at Las Médulas while raising unmortared double-tiered granite aqueducts at Segovia.
entries.detail: UNESCO dossier No. 803 and Deming (2019) quantify Roman hydraulic engineering applied to both urban water supply and industrial placer gold extraction.
entries.uncertainty: Total gold tonnages mined across Asturian valleys come from Pliny's literary estimates rather than surviving imperial ledgers.

entries.title: Guadalquivir estates ship millions of Dressel 20 olive-oil amphorae to Rome
entries.dateMeaning: Timestamped Baetican estate *tituli picti* on shards at Rome's Monte Testaccio
entries.summary: Stamped spherical amphorae loaded down the Guadalquivir supplied Rome's public olive-oil annona, piling 50+ million broken vessels into Monte Testaccio.
entries.detail: Komar et al. (2025) and Castillo Pascual (2023) demonstrate how Baetica's river-sea network sustained Mediterranean bulk food trade for two and a half centuries.
entries.uncertainty: Linear trade vector represents river-maritime transport from Seville across western Mediterranean lanes to Ostia/Portus.

entries.title: Northeastern Hispania transitions from Iberian oppida to municipal Roman towns
entries.dateMeaning: Archaeodemographic transformation from late Iberian hillforts to Flavian municipia
entries.summary: Planned orthogonal Roman cities such as Barcino and Tarraco replaced fortified coastal *oppida*, expanding regional population and Flavian municipal citizenship.
entries.detail: Sinner & Carreras Monfort (2019) combine roofed residential footprints and urban plans across Catalonia to calibrate demographic densities.
entries.uncertainty: Early oppida household multipliers vary slightly compared with imperial Italian insulae models.

entries.title: Umayyad Córdoba and Nasrid Granada create irrigated urban capitals of Al-Andalus
entries.dateMeaning: Umayyad conquest to 1492 surrender of Granada
entries.summary: Hydraulic waterwheels, mosque-university libraries in caliphal Córdoba, and terraced palaces in Nasrid Granada anchored one of medieval Europe's richest urban regions.
entries.detail: Curta (2011), Martins (2025), and UNESCO dossiers 313 and 314 synthesize Islamic–Christian frontier urbanization and agrarian innovation.
entries.uncertainty: Population spikes for tenth-century Córdoba involve retrospective medieval chronicler approximations.

entries.title: Medieval Barcelona and Catalan municipalities forge representative Mediterranean estates
entries.dateMeaning: Aragonese Crown maritime expansion from chartered coastal *universitats* to 1492
entries.summary: Commercial merchant elites forged municipal councils (*Consell de Cent*), Mediterranean maritime consulates, and parliamentary Corts alongside Aragonese kings.
entries.detail: Sabaté (2021) traces how Catalan bourgeois institutions anchored western Mediterranean trade from Valencia to Sicily.
entries.uncertainty: Fourteenth-century plague and civil conflict caused pronounced demographic contractions prior to early modern rebuilding.

entries.title: Seville's Casa de la Contratación steers transoceanic silver and Atlantic commerce
entries.dateMeaning: Establishment of the House of Trade at Seville (1503) through 1717 transfer to Cádiz and mid-18th c.
entries.summary: Chartered as the royal monopoly port for the Americas, Seville drew Basque shipwrights, Genoese bankers, African enslaved captives, and Asian textiles.
entries.detail: McClure (2020) and Buringh (2021) chart Seville's institutional transformation into an early modern world emporium.
entries.uncertainty: Guadalquivir sandbars increasingly shifted deep-draft fleets downriver toward Cádiz after the 1680s.

entries.title: Iberian-gauge trunk railways radiate outward from Madrid across mountain passes
entries.dateMeaning: Opening of peninsula's first rail segment (1848) through General Railway Act construction wave
entries.place: Madrid Atocha/Príncipe Pío to Barcelona port corridor
entries.summary: Following the 1848 Barcelona–Mataró line and 1851 Madrid–Aranjuez route, foreign and state capital drove a Madrid-centered Iberian broad-gauge trunk web.
entries.detail: Martí-Romero et al. (2021) and Esteban-Oliver & Martí-Henneberg (2024) analyze the radial structure and mountainous terrain barriers shaping Spanish rail integration.
entries.uncertainty: Non-standard 1,672 mm Iberian track gauge required transshipment at the French Pyrenean border.

entries.title: INE censuses document Madrid almost doubling to 575,675 inhabitants between 1857 and 1900
entries.dateMeaning: Official Spanish national census enumerations in 1857, 1877, 1887, and 1900
entries.summary: Supported by Castro's planned Ensanche suburbs and converging radial rail trunks, Madrid grew from 298,638 in 1857 to 419,243 in 1877, 495,063 in 1887, and 575,675 in 1900.
entries.detail: Álvarez-Palau et al. (2019) and INE municipal series trace Spain's modern urban density shift around the national capital.
entries.uncertainty: Municipal Ensanche urbanization proceeded block by block inside the 1860 master plan perimeter.

entries.title: INE censuses chart steady nineteenth-century growth in Seville (112,529 to 147,271)
entries.dateMeaning: Official Spanish national census series for Seville (1857, 1877, 1887, 1900)
entries.summary: Andalusia's river port climbed from 112,529 inhabitants in 1857 to 133,247 in 1877, 143,840 in 1887, and 147,271 by the 1900 census.
entries.detail: INE historical tables paired with Álvarez-Palau et al. (2019) contrast Seville's moderate post-colonial demographic expansion with booming northern rail hubs.
entries.uncertainty: Seasonal rural agricultural labor fluctuated around fixed municipal census reference dates.

entries.title: Industrial Barcelona expands from 183,787 (1857) to 533,000 (1900) via the Cerdà Eixample and 1897 annexations
entries.dateMeaning: Pre-annexation 1857 and 1887 municipal counts paired with post-1897 expanded city total in 1900
entries.summary: Demolishing medieval walls in 1854 for Ildefons Cerdà's grid, Barcelona rose from 183,787 (1857) and 272,481 (1887) before sweeping 1897 plain annexations lifted it to 533,000 in 1900.
entries.detail: Álvarez-Palau et al. (2019) examine Spanish industrial urban expansion; because Barcelona annexed six surrounding manufacturing towns (Gràcia, Sants, Sant Andreu, etc.) in 1897, these checkpoints distinguish pre- and post-annexation boundaries.
entries.uncertainty: Boundary discontinuous after the April 1897 annexation of neighboring industrial communes; intermediate years are not linearly interpolated.

entries.title: Gruta da Aroeira yields ~400 ka Middle Pleistocene cranium with Acheulean handaxes
entries.dateMeaning: U-series speleothem crust age tightly bracketing the Aroeira 3 cranium
entries.place: Almonda Karst System, Torres Novas, Portugal
entries.summary: Hardened breccia above the Almonda spring held a partial Acheulean-associated human skull (Aroeira 3), burnt bones, and stone bifaces.
entries.detail: Daura et al. (2017) directly dated overlaying stalagmites via U-series, providing Europe's westernmost dated Middle Pleistocene human cranium.
entries.uncertainty: Calcified breccia cementation obscures fine suture detail across damaged facial elements.

entries.title: Last Interglacial Neanderthals harvest Atlantic crabs and shellfish at Figueira Brava
entries.dateMeaning: OSL and U-series carbonate ages across coastal Mousterian sea-cave levels
entries.place: Serra da Arrábida, Setúbal peninsula, Portugal
entries.summary: Beside the Atlantic surf, Neanderthals roasted brown crabs, limpets, tortoises, pine nuts, and marine seals in quantities rivaling early African coastal sites.
entries.detail: Nabais et al. (2023) demonstrate structured Last Interglacial Atlantic foraging and roasted crab processing on Portugal's coast.
entries.uncertainty: Rising post-glacial ocean submerged lower intertidal shelves outside the surviving elevated cave chambers.

entries.title: Lapa do Picareiro pushes modern human Aurignacian arrival in Portugal to ~41–38 ka
entries.dateMeaning: AMS radiocarbon dates on herbivore bones from Aurignacian Level GG
entries.place: Serra de Aire, Estremadura, central Portugal
entries.summary: Deep upland karst levels preserve bladelet diagnostics linking Atlantic Portugal within millennia of Central European Aurignacian dispersals.
entries.detail: Haws et al. (2020) documented stratified Aurignacian bladelets beneath intact Solutrean deposits, narrowing the chronological offset along the Atlantic margin.
entries.uncertainty: Level GG lacks diagnostic human skeletal fossils alongside its Aurignacian stone assemblage.

entries.title: Hunters peck thousands of open-air Paleolithic engravings along Côa Valley schists
entries.dateMeaning: Stratified river terrace excavations and luminescence ages at Fariseu
entries.place: Vila Nova de Foz Côa (Douro Basin), NE Portugal
entries.summary: Rather than retreating exclusively underground, Iberian Upper Paleolithic groups engraved towering herds of aurochs, horses, and ibex directly on sunlit river cliffs.
entries.detail: Preserved under UNESCO dossier No. 866 alongside Siega Verde and framed by Villalba-Mouco et al. (2023), the Côa canyon holds Europe's grandest open-air Ice Age art sanctuary.
entries.uncertainty: Bare rock faces expose engravings to superimposition across Gravettian, Solutrean, and Magdalenian phases.

entries.title: Copper Age Atlantic communities erect the corbelled Alcalar tholos necropolis in Algarve
entries.dateMeaning: Comparative southern Portuguese megalithic tholos mound and slate-plaque typology
entries.summary: Monumental dry-stone corbelled passage chambers and fortified hill settlements anchored southwestern Iberian Atlantic copper-and-shell networks.
entries.detail: Arnaiz-Villena et al. (2022) inspect stone engravings and monumental architecture linking Atlantic Algarve complexes across Iberian Copper Age landscapes.
entries.uncertainty: Many eighteenth- and nineteenth-century openings disturbed original sealed chamber stratigraphies.

entries.title: Sixteenth-century Lisbon transforms the Tagus estuary into a global oceanic capital
entries.dateMeaning: Indian Ocean pepper armadas opening (~1500) to Pombaline rebuilding after the 1755 earthquake
entries.place: Ribeira das Naus & Belém, Tagus estuary, Lisbon
entries.summary: Receiving Malacca cloves, Indian pepper, West African gold, and Brazilian sugar, Lisbon expanded into Europe's Atlantic–Indian exchange hub.
entries.detail: Bermejo (2016) compares early modern imperial Lisbon with Papal Rome as multi-ethnic harbor communities, arsenals, and convents reshaped the Tagus shoreline.
entries.uncertainty: Pre-earthquake parish books suffered catastrophic archive losses in the November 1755 fire and tsunami.

entries.title: Lines of Torres Vedras halt Masséna's French invasion north of Lisbon
entries.dateMeaning: Secret construction of fortified belts across 1809–1810 through French retreat in 1811
entries.place: Torres Vedras – Tagus – Atlantic fortified belt, Portugal
entries.summary: Over 150 mutually supporting redoubts across steep ridges north of Lisbon starved Napoleon's Peninsular army without fighting a pitched assault.
entries.detail: Part of Black's (1999) late Napoleonic continental conflicts, Anglo-Portuguese positional engineering preserved Atlantic supply lines via Lisbon harbor.
entries.uncertainty: Civilian scorched-earth displacement figures across central Portuguese districts remain broad historical approximations.

participants: French Imperial Army of Portugal under Marshal Masséna
warfare.outcome: French starvation and withdrawal out of central Portugal paved the way for 1812–1814 Allied campaigns into Spain.

entries.title: Portuguese broad-gauge trunk rail reaches the Spanish border and Madrid
entries.dateMeaning: First Portuguese steam railway line (1856) through cross-border Madrid link in 1863–1866
entries.place: Lisbon Santa Apolónia to Spanish border / Madrid trunk
entries.summary: Adopting the same 1,668/1,672 mm broad-gauge standard as Spain, Portugal's Leste trunk tied Tagus Atlantic docks directly onto Madrid's rail web.
entries.detail: Esteban-Oliver & Martí-Henneberg (2024) map Iberian peninsula cross-border integration from isolated Tagus lines toward Madrid-bound trunks.
entries.uncertainty: Early international passenger traffic relied on seasonal river bridges before masonry Tagus viaducts stabilized capacity.

entries.title: Lisbon grows from ~200,000 in 1864 to 356,009 in 1900 under Portuguese censuses
entries.dateMeaning: Mid-century 1864 baseline (~200,000 within period boundaries) and official 1890 & 1900 censuses
entries.summary: Expanding onto the northern Avenida da Liberdade plateau after industrial ports and railways consolidated, Lisbon grew from 300,964 (1890) to 356,009 (1900).
entries.detail: INE Portugal decennial enumerations reflect post-1886 municipal limits unifying industrial eastern wharves and northern suburban parishes.
entries.uncertainty: Earlier 1864 figures used narrower pre-1885 parish boundaries; only 1890–1900 censuses share comparable post-1886 municipal borders.

population.note: Approximate 1864 rounded baseline prior to 1886 municipal expansion.
